entities.summary:
Kim Si-min (d. 1592), a distinguished general of the Joseon Dynasty, stands as a pivotal figure in Korean military history, primarily remembered for his heroic defense of Jinju Castle against overwhelming Japanese forces during the Imjin War (1592-1598), also known as the Seven Years' War. His strategic brilliance and unyielding resolve at Jinju in late 1592 temporarily halted the Japanese advance into the southwestern provinces, safeguarding a crucial granary region and bolstering Korean morale at a critical juncture when the kingdom faced existential threat. Born into the influential (old) Andong Kim clan, his actions transcended mere military success, embodying the spirit of resistance that ultimately prevented the complete subjugation of Joseon Korea.

In October 1592, following the initial Japanese invasion that had seen the fall of Seoul and Pyongyang, Kim Si-min, then the Right Gyeongsang Provincial Army Commander, prepared Jinju Castle for a siege. With a vastly outnumbered force, estimated at around 3,800 Korean defenders against a Japanese army of some 20,000 to 30,000, he employed innovative defensive tactics, including the use of hwacha (multiple rocket launchers) and newly designed cannons. For six days, from October 27 to November 3, 1592, Kim Si-min led his troops in fierce resistance, repelling multiple frontal assaults and inflicting heavy casualties on the besiegers, critically disrupting the Japanese supply lines and their strategic objectives to secure the fertile Honam region.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Kim Si-min's successful defense of Jinju Castle in 1592 was a pivotal moment in the Imjin War, preventing the Japanese from securing vital granaries and significantly boosting Joseon morale. His actions bought critical time for Joseon and Ming forces to regroup, altering the war's trajectory.
